title: Principles of Mixed-Initiative User Interfaces
claim: Resolve key uncertainty through dialogue while considering interruption cost; permit direct control and refinement.
limitations: Not a controlled creative-brief experiment or a universal numerical questioning threshold.

title: Requirements Engineering: A Roadmap
claim: Elicitation combines existing-document analysis, questions, observation and prototypes; method depends on information needed.
context: Software stakeholders, purposes and evolving requirements.
limitations: Not evidence for one standardized creative interview; paying client and end users may differ.

title: Techniques for Requirements Elicitation
claim: Predetermined questions and designer introspection can miss meaning and tacit context.
context: Workplace systems and socially situated requirements.
limitations: Theoretical/methodological argument with examples, not an experimental comparison of all methods.

title: Co-creation and the new landscapes of design
locator: Introduction; definition of co-design; fuzzy-front-end discussion
claim: People can participate in informing, ideating and conceptualizing rather than only evaluating others' concepts.
limitations: Conceptual advocacy, not proof that one owner represents users or that every person wants every design responsibility; later section fetches timed out.

title: Frame Your Design Challenge
claim: Frame outcome, audience, context and constraints while retaining multiple possible solutions.
limitations: Prescribed workshop duration and solution-count exercise are context-specific, not universal chat requirements.

title: Conversation Starters
claim: Use disposable concepts to spark reactions and follow the participant's interpretation.
limitations: Provocative prompts are not neutral measurement or commitments; no causal outcome study supplied.

title: Using in-depth interviews
locator: Design the interview; Do the interview; After the interview
claim: Use open neutral prompts, specific examples and adaptive follow-ups rather than rigidly following a guide.
context: Research participants and actual service experience.
limitations: A project-owner creative conversation is not automatically end-user research; not a rule against all closed questions.

title: Parallel Prototyping Leads to Better Design Results, More Divergence, and Increased Self-Efficacy
locator: §3.1–3.4 method; Introduction results; discussion of critique
claim: Parallel alternatives improved several outcomes in a bounded web-ad design task.
context: 33 nonprofessional designers; matched total prototypes, feedback and time; one client.
limitations: Not evidence for a mandatory count or approval after each screen; experimenter-selected critique and ad metrics limit transfer.

title: Getting the Right Design and the Design Right: Testing Many Is Better Than One
claim: Alternative prototypes changed ratings and criticism without significantly increasing substantial redesign suggestions.
context: 48 students/recent graduates; one versus three thermostat paper prototypes.
limitations: Small task-specific study; lower ratings do not by themselves prove greater truth; alternatives are not a substitute for design expertise.

title: Preference-based Search using Example-Critiquing with Suggestions
evidence_type: formal model, simulations and user studies
claim: Critiquing varied examples can reveal preferences absent from an initial request.
context: Apartment-search interface; supervised within-subject study with40 mostly undergraduate participants.
limitations: Finite catalog and operationalized preferred choice; transfer to open-ended visual creation is a proposal, not demonstrated.

title: Clarify When Necessary: Resolving Ambiguity Through Interaction with LMs
claim: Useful clarification concerns errors that the answer can actually resolve, not uncertainty alone.
context: QA, translation and inference tasks; annotation-derived oracle questions/answers.
limitations: Not a live creative-user study; interaction cost modeled as a budget rather than measured human effort.

title: Deciding Whether to Ask Clarifying Questions in Large-Scale Spoken Language Understanding
claim: Context and alternative hypotheses help distinguish consequential ambiguity from redundant clarification.
context: Five spoken-language ambiguity categories and real commercial agent data.
limitations: Offline classifier outcomes do not prove a creative-brief dialogue policy or aesthetic quality.

title: Asking Clarifying Questions: To Benefit or to Disturb Users in Web Search?
evidence_type: empirical search-user study, partial methods access
source_family: Zou et al. / conversational information retrieval
locator: Original abstract/introduction; manuscript metadata; later method fetches timed out
claim: Reported question-quality trajectories affect user behavior and satisfaction.
limitations: Method details incompletely retrieved; no effect magnitude or universal timing/count rule adopted.

title: Grounding in Communication
locator: Grounding criterion; Least Collaborative Effort; Grounding Changes with Purpose/Medium
claim: Shared understanding only needs to suffice for the current purpose; minimize combined communication effort.
limitations: Applying this theory to a coding agent's state tracking is our design proposal.

title: Design Fixation
evidence_type: original experiment abstract; scanned-paper access gap
locator: Publisher abstract; university PDF text extraction/screenshot transport insufficient for full-method verification
claim: Original abstract reports experiments demonstrating example-related fixation.
limitations: No detailed experimental count/effect or blanket ban on references adopted.

title: Ask Before or After? Clarification Timing and User Experience in Generative AI
source_family: Jung et al. / Creativity and Cognition
locator: Publisher-indexed abstract and result excerpts; DOI/fullHTML403
claim: Reported30-person study compares question presence/timing and perceived effort/trust.
limitations: Full study protocol inaccessible; confidence/trust is not demonstrated accuracy; no exact effect used.

title: Co-Creation Session
claim: Participants can make and reshape concepts; capture feedback and treat them as collaborators.
limitations: No quantitative adoption claim accepted; workshop recipe is not a mandatory AI approval loop.
